content: Acacia mellifera is a perennial tree that is not currently classified as a threatened species. The species name mellifera is derived from its sweet-smelling blossoms, which are associated with honey production. When its wood is treated with oil, it turns a deep pitch black color. This tree is commonly referred to as Blackthorn or Swaarthaak in Afrikaans. Acacia mellifera is distributed across arid regions of Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, Australia, India, and areas surrounding the Indian Ocean. This species can grow either as a multi-stemmed shrub, reaching heights of up to seven meters, with a crown that is somewhat funnel-shaped, or as a small single-stemmed tree that can grow as tall as nine meters. It reproduces both through seed production and vegetative propagation via root suckers, which can result in dense, impenetrable thickets containing hundreds of individual plants. In the dry regions of Africa, Acacia mellifera serves multiple purposes. It is used as fencing material, livestock feed, and as a construction material for huts. The nectar from its blossoms is occasionally consumed as food. Medicinally, the milky sap of the tree is used as an emetic to induce vomiting, while the boiled bark is employed in the treatment of abdominal pain, pneumonia, and malaria. This tree is a vital source of nutrition for both livestock and wildlife, particularly in the arid regions of Africa. Its leaves and young branches are highly nutritious, containing a significant amount of protein. The flowers are a favored food source for kudu. Other animals that commonly browse on this tree include black rhinoceroses, giraffes, and elands. There are two recognized subspecies of Acacia mellifera: Acacia mellifera (Vahl) Benth subsp. detinens (Burchell) Brenan Acacia mellifera (Vahl) Benth subsp. mellifera
